_README: Verified civic-data sources for every Expose chapter. This file is the audit trail.
EVERY url in this file returned a live 2xx (or a 3xx whose target was followed and
recorded) on the date in `verified`. Nothing here was recalled from memory, guessed
from a URL pattern, or copied from a search-result snippet without being fetched.
That rule is the whole point: the sites built from this file tell residents where to
file, and a wrong link is worse than no link.
`portal` is the machine-readable meeting source and drives the weekly ingest.
Vendors and the ingest script that speaks to each:
primegov    ingest_primegov.py     JSON API, agendas + video in one record
legistar    ingest_legistar.py     webapi.legistar.com OData, agenda PDFs
wordpress   ingest_wordpress.py    wp-json custom post type
`issue` follows the rule already established for the state-hub expansion queues:
name the STRUCTURAL question and the specific public record that answers it. Never
assert that a named city has a scandal we have not documented. A chapter's index
page gets rewritten around a documented fact once the records come back.

oversight.label: Oklahoma Attorney General
oversight.note: Issues Open Records Act opinions. Oklahoma has no free citizen appeal forum — enforcement is a district-court action under § 24A.17.

oversight.label: Oklahoma State Auditor & Inspector
oversight.note: Audits every county and, on petition or request, municipalities. Published audits are public records.

oversight.label: Texas Attorney General — Open Government
oversight.note: A body that wants to withhold must ask the AG within 10 business days. Those rulings are public and searchable, and they are the single best record of what a city tried to hide.

oversight.label: Texas Comptroller — Transparency
oversight.note: Local government debt, tax rates and economic-development agreements, filed by the entities themselves.

oversight.label: Mississippi Ethics Commission
oversight.note: A denial appeals here FREE under § 25-61-13. The Commission can order release and fine the official who wrongfully withheld. This is the strongest citizen remedy of the three states.

oversight.label: Mississippi Office of the State Auditor
oversight.note: Audits municipalities and counties; published reports are public records.

issue.headline: Where the MAPS money actually lands
issue.body: Oklahoma City's MAPS programme is a voter-approved sales tax that has moved well over a billion dollars through successive rounds, and the state capital runs the largest economic-development incentive book in Oklahoma. The structural question is not whether the projects happened — it is which contracts, change orders and incentive agreements carry the spend, and those are records the City holds.
issue.record: MAPS contract and change-order files, and the economic-development agreements approved by resolution, requested by date range from the City Clerk.

issue.headline: TIF districts, and who is inside them
issue.body: Tulsa is Oklahoma's second metro and runs an extensive tax-increment finance programme alongside county jail and detention contracting. A TIF district diverts future property tax off the general roll for decades; the increment schedule and the participation agreements are public, and they say precisely who benefits and for how long.
issue.record: TIF project plans and participation agreements, plus the annual increment reports filed with the County Assessor.

issue.headline: A small city with a utility, an authority, and no newsroom
issue.body: Claremore runs its own municipal utility and a set of public trusts and authorities that meet separately from the Council. Small cities are not less accountable because less happens — they are less accountable because nobody attends. The agendas are posted 48 hours ahead under the Open Meeting Act; almost nobody reads them.
issue.record: Claremore Public Works Authority and Industrial/Economic Development Authority agendas, minutes and utility rate ordinances.

issue.headline: The largest city in Texas, and the AG rulings it asks for
issue.body: Houston is the biggest public body in the state, and under the Public Information Act a body that wants to withhold must ask the Attorney General within ten business days and say why. Those requests and the rulings on them are themselves public. The pattern of what a city routinely asks permission to withhold is a map of what it does not want read.
issue.record: Attorney General open-records rulings naming the City of Houston, cross-referenced against the City's own GovQA request log.

issue.headline: Every vote, tied to the money that preceded it
issue.body: Dallas publishes its agendas, minutes and roll-call votes through Legistar as structured data — which means the record of who voted for what is machine-readable, and can be lined up against the contract awards and zoning cases on the same agenda. Very little of that comparison has ever been done in public.
issue.record: Legistar roll-call votes and matter histories, joined to the contract award items on the same agenda.

issue.headline: A city that publishes a lot, and what still is not in it
issue.body: Austin is unusually good at publishing — eDIMS, an open-data portal, a full Legistar instance, a televised archive going back decades. That makes it the right place to ask the harder question: with all of that published, which categories of record still require a request, and what do the AG rulings say the City asked to withhold anyway.
issue.record: Attorney General open-records rulings naming the City of Austin, read against what eDIMS already publishes.

issue.headline: CPS Energy and SAWS answer to the city, and to no voter directly
issue.body: San Antonio owns its electric and gas utility and its water system. Their boards are appointed, not elected, and their rate cases, fuel-cost recoveries and capital plans move more money than most line items in the City budget. They are public bodies, so their board packets are public records.
issue.record: CPS Energy and San Antonio Water System board packets, rate-case filings and the annual transfer to the City's general fund.

issue.headline: A city that owns its power company, on a shrinking aquifer
issue.body: Lubbock runs a municipal electric utility and sits on the Ogallala. Industrial load growth — including data-centre-scale load — lands on ratepayers through the utility rather than through the tax roll, which means the decision that raises a household bill is made in a utility board packet, not in a budget hearing.
issue.record: Lubbock Power & Light board agendas and rate ordinances, and the City's water supply and wholesale-power contracts.

issue.headline: The same West Texas water basin as San Angelo
issue.body: Abilene draws from the same stressed West Texas supply as the Foundation's first Texas chapter, and is courting the same category of large industrial water and power customer. San Angelo's chapter exists because the water numbers were in the City's own records the whole time. Abilene's are too.
issue.record: Raw-water contracts, reservoir and well-field yield reports, and any industrial water-service agreement approved by the Council.

issue.headline: A water system under federal oversight, and a contracting record that is public
issue.body: Jackson's water system has been under federal oversight, which produced something unusual: a court-supervised paper trail running alongside the City's own procurement. The Mississippi Public Records Act gives a resident seven working days and a free appeal to the Ethics Commission — the strongest citizen remedy of the three states this Foundation works in, and almost nobody uses it.
issue.record: Water system contracts and change orders, the interim manager's filed reports, and Council appropriations tied to each.

issue.headline: The other side of the DeSoto County tax base
issue.body: Olive Branch shares a county, a tax base, a water table and an industrial corridor with Southaven — where an ad valorem tax agreement abating two thirds of property tax on a recital of twenty new jobs is already published in full on this Foundation's Mississippi chapter. The same agreements, the same aquifer and the same board structure exist here, and no one has asked for them.
issue.record: Ad valorem tax exemption agreements approved by the Board of Aldermen, and the City's water-well permits and monthly pumpage reports.

founding_archives._source: Counted directly on the serving containers 2026-07-27: `find /var/www/<chapter>/html/meetings -maxdepth 1 -type d` and siblings. These three chapters predate the weekly pipeline and do not publish a generated meetings.json, so their totals cannot be read the way the other eleven are. Recount with the same commands before quoting these anywhere.
